passage: I'm Rekha, and that night I was the one on the status page. Every thirty minutes I posted a short update: what we knew, what we didn't, and when the next one would come. Zubin, who was leading the fix, sent me two lines at a time and I turned them into plain words. The first update said only, 'Payments are slow, we're looking into it, next update at nine forty.' Not glamorous, but at nine forty I posted again, even when the news was 'still working on it'. What surprised me was the support inbox. It had been flooding, and after the third update the messages slowed. One customer wrote, 'Thanks for actually telling us.' I was nervous the whole time, but I learned that people can bear bad news better than silence.

qa.q: How often did Rekha post an update?
qa.a: Rekha posted an update every thirty minutes.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel during the outage?
qa.a: Rekha was nervous the whole time, though the customer thanks brought some relief. 🙂

qa.q: What other approach could Rekha add if the cause stayed unknown for hours?
qa.a: Rekha could also message the biggest customers directly, since a public page may not be enough for people who depend on the service most.

qa.q: How might a customer have felt after reading the third update?
qa.a: A customer would likely feel calmer and respected, since one wrote 'Thanks for actually telling us.'

grounding: Shows a communications owner posting short honest updates on a regular schedule with the next update time, which eased customer worry.
